'''John Charles Warner''' (born October 25, 1962) is an American [[List of chemists|chemist]], [[Teacher|educator]], and entrepreneur, best known as one of the founders of the field of [[green chemistry]]. Warner worked in [[Private industry|industry]] for nearly a decade as a researcher at [[Polaroid Corporation]], before moving to [[Academy|academia]] where he worked in various positions at [[University of Massachusetts Boston]] and [[University of Massachusetts Lowell|Lowell]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/90/i34/John-Warner.html|title=John Warner {{!}} August 20, 2012, Issue – Vol. 90 Issue 34 {{!}} Chemical & Engineering News|last=Hogue|first=Cheryl|website=cen.acs.org|access-date=November 10, 2017}}</ref> Warner is co-founder, President, and Chief Technology Officer at the Warner-Babcock Institute for Green Chemistry, as well as co-founder and President of Beyond Benign. He is the recipient of the 2014 [[Perkin Medal]], widely acknowledged as the highest honor in American industrial chemistry.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chemistry.princeton.edu/news/princeton-chemistry-alumnus-john-c-warner-receives-2014-perkin-medal|title=Princeton chemistry alumnus John C. Warner receives 2014 Perkin Medal {{!}} Princeton University Department of Chemistry|website=chemistry.princeton.edu|language=en|access-date=November 10, 2017}}</ref>

== Education ==
Warner was born in [[Quincy, Massachusetts]], to John A. and Natalie Warner as part of a huge family, including 47 first cousins within a one-mile radius.<ref name=":12">{{Citation|last=Green Builder Media|title=Green Chemistry, The Missing Element|date=January 18, 2017|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g5cTD_MaCIc|access-date=October 21, 2017}}</ref> During his childhood, Warner first met his long-time friend and colleague [[Paul Anastas]] at age eleven, with whom he later co-authored the defining work in the developing field, ''Green Chemistry: Theory and Practice.''<ref name=":22">{{Citation|last=Collaborative Aggregates LLC|title=MPPP Annual Meeting: John Warner, Green Chemistry: The Missing Elements|date=December 16, 2015|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RuIqnSDU-sI|access-date=October 21, 2017}}</ref>

Anastas and Warner both attended [[Quincy High School (Massachusetts)|Quincy High School]], where Warner was most well known, not as a [[chemist]], but as a musician.<ref name=":72">{{Citation|last=Collaborative Aggregates LLC|title=Dr. John Warner: Green Chemistry & Commercial Applications|date=December 8, 2016|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3UEI8-NTH00|access-date=December 1, 2017}}</ref> There, he played in the marching band and the jazz band, and was voted class musician.<ref name=":12" /> No one in Warner's family at the time had attended university, and most of them worked as [[Tradesman|tradespeople]], but Warner ultimately decided to attend [[University of Massachusetts Boston]], where Anastas also matriculated, as a music major.<ref name=":12" /> Warner worked in construction full-time to pay his own tuition throughout college.<ref name=":72" /> He played in a successful band called the Elements until the death of drummer James "Opie" Neil, at which point Warner became more much involved in his then-elective chemistry classes.<ref name=":12" /> He began doing research in the laboratory of Jean-Pierre Anselme, where Anastas also worked, and this ultimately inspired him to switch majors.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Warner|first1=John C.|last2=Anastas|first2=Paul T.|last3=Anselme|first3=Jean-Pierre|date=April 1, 1985|title=The Wittig reaction in the undergraduate organic laboratory|journal=Journal of Chemical Education|volume=62|issue=4|pages=346|doi=10.1021/ed062p346|bibcode=1985JChEd..62..346W|issn=0021-9584}}</ref> He published five papers as an undergraduate by the time he was twenty years old.<ref name=":12" /> Warner graduated alongside Anastas, receiving his B.S. in chemistry in 1984.<ref name=":04">{{Cite news|url=http://www.warnerbabcock.com/people/john-warner-ph-d/|title=John Warner – Warner Babcock Institute|work=Warner Babcock Institute|access-date=October 21, 2017|language=en-US}}</ref>

After college, Warner pursued graduate studies at [[Princeton University]], where he received a PhD in chemistry after completing a doctoral dissertation, titled "Synthesis of pyrido[2,3-d]pyrimidines (5-deazapteridines)", under the supervision of [[Edward C. Taylor]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Warner|first=John Charles|url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/445066|title=Synthesis of pyrido[2,3-d]pyrimidines (5-deazapteridines)|date=1988|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":04" /> His group helped synthesize [[pemetrexed]] (brand name Alimta), one of the most powerful anti-cancer drugs for solid tumors.<ref name=":22" />

== Career ==
Warner was offered a job immediately after graduate school in research and development at [[Polaroid Corporation]], where he worked for almost a decade.<ref name=":72" /> During this time, Warner first conceived a theory called Non-Covalent [[Derivatization]], a unique approach to chemical synthesis that involves changing the properties of a target [[material]] by exploiting its innate [[intermolecular force]]s. It was also while working for Polaroid that Warner was reunited with childhood and undergraduate friend [[Paul Anastas]], then employed at the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]], at a meeting that inspired Warner to co-author his most influential work ''Green Chemistry: Theory and Practice'' with Anastas.<ref name=":22" />

In 1996, Warner returned to academia to work at [[University of Massachusetts Boston]], where he served as tenured full professor as well as chair of the department of chemistry from 2001 to 2003.<ref name=":04" /> It was also there that he established the world's first PhD program in Green Chemistry. Amy Cannon, whom he later married, was the program's first graduate and the first person to receive a PhD in the field of Green Chemistry.<ref name=":3" /> He then moved to [[University of Massachusetts Lowell]], where he established and directed the Center for Green Chemistry from 2004 to 2007.<ref name=":22" />

Warner left Lowell in 2007 to co-found, with investment firm executive Jim Babcock, the Warner-Babcock Institute for Green Chemistry, and, with his wife Amy Cannon, Beyond Benign, a nonprofit organization for green chemistry education.<ref name=":3" />

Committed to educating the public on green chemistry, Warner has spoken as keynote and plenary speaker for numerous green chemistry and [[sustainability]] conferences. Aside from awards for his work in the field, he was selected (with Anastas) as a "Top 40 Power Player" by ICIS in 2008,<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.icis.com/resources/news/2008/12/08/9177358/the-2008-icis-top-40/ | title=The 2008 ICIS Top 40}}</ref> and as an [[Utne Reader]] "visionary" in 2011.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.utne.com/science-and-technology/utne-reader-visionaries-john-warner-green-chemist.aspx | title=John Warner: Green Chemist — Visionaries — Utne Reader| date=October 10, 2011}}</ref>

Warner has invented technologies for companies including Nike, Givaudan, Covestro, Lanxess, and Entegris, as serving on advisory boards for companies including Dow, Nike, Levis, and Apple. In 2022, he took up the role of Distinguished Research Fellow at DUDE CHEM, Berlin<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team |url=https://www.dudechem.com/gallery |access-date=2023-01-31 |website=DUDE CHEM |language=en-US}}</ref> and as Green Chemistry Innovation Advisor at GL Chemtec, Ontario.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-11-08 |title=GL CHEMTEC Appoints Dr. John Warner as Green Chemistry Innovation Advisor |url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20221108006209/en/GL-CHEMTEC-Appoints-Dr.-John-Warner-as-Green-Chemistry-Innovation-Advisor |access-date=2023-01-31 |website=www.businesswire.com |language=en}}</ref> In 2024, Warner was appointed [[professor of practice]] at the [[Rochester Institute of Technology]] (RIT).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Golisano Institute for Sustainability |date=September 24, 2024 |title=John Warner, co-founder of green chemistry, named professor of practice |url=https://www.rit.edu/news/john-warner-co-founder-green-chemistry-named-professor-practice |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240925153535/https://www.rit.edu/news/john-warner-co-founder-green-chemistry-named-professor-practice |archive-date=2024-09-25 |access-date=2024-09-25 |website=RIT |language=en}}</ref>

== Non-Covalent Derivatization ==
Warner first articulated the concept of Non-Covalent [[Derivatization]] (NCD) at a conference in 1997,<ref>{{Cite book|title=Proceedings of the IS&T's 50th Annual Conference|last1=Guarrera|first1=D.J.|last2=Kingsley|first2=E.|last3=Taylor|first3=L.D.|last4=Warner|first4=John C.|year=1997}}</ref> but he employed this concept in practice as early as 1988.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Muehldorf|first1=Alexander V.|last2=Van Engen|first2=Donna.|last3=Warner|first3=John C.|last4=Hamilton|first4=Andrew D.|date=September 1, 1988|title=Aromatic-aromatic interactions in molecular recognition: a family of artificial receptors for thymine that shows both face-to-face and edge-to-face orientations|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=110|issue=19|pages=6561–6562|doi=10.1021/ja00227a045|bibcode=1988JAChS.110.6561M |issn=0002-7863}}</ref> He initially devised this method as a solution to a common engineering problem that [[Hydroquinone|hydroquinone (HQ)]], an essential developer in [[Polaroid camera|Polaroid]] [[instant photography]], is not readily [[Solubility|soluble]] in water. HQ is desired in more modern applications for its potency as a [[reducing agent]], and until Warner, this problem was typically addressed by traditional chemical synthesis, or modifying a target material by attaching various [[functional group]]s via [[covalent bond]]s, also referred to as "covalent derivatization."<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Noncovalent derivatives of hydroquinone: bis-(N,N-dialkyl)bicyclo[2.2.2]octane-1,4-dicarboxamide complexes|journal=Crystal Engineering|volume=2|pages=55–64|doi=10.1016/S1463-0184(99)00007-6|year=1999|last1=Foxman|first1=Bruce M.|last2=Guarrera|first2=Donna J.|last3=Pai|first3=Ramdas|last4=Tassa|first4=Carlos|last5=Warner|first5=John C.|issue=1 |bibcode=1999CrEng...2...55F }}</ref> [[Biomimetics|Inspired by phenomena he observed in nature]], Warner proposed NCD as an alternative means of modifying a target material, not via covalent bonds, but innate [[intermolecular force]]s.<ref name=":22" />

In the model example of hydroquinone, Warner devised a novel process of [[Cocrystal|co-crystallization]] between HQ and a terephthalamide molecule, which yielded a product complex that was much more soluble in water than HQ alone.<ref name=":52">{{Cite journal|last1=Cannon|first1=Amy S.|last2=Warner|first2=John C.|date=July 1, 2002|title=Noncovalent Derivatization: Green Chemistry Applications of Crystal Engineering|journal=Crystal Growth & Design|volume=2|issue=4|pages=255–257|doi=10.1021/cg0255218|bibcode=2002CrGrD...2..255C |issn=1528-7483}}</ref> The applications of this process ranged from [[Photographic processing|film development]] to more recently [[Cosmetics|cosmetic]] [[dermatology]]. NCD is now most often employed as an effective means of reducing the [[Environmental issue|environmental impact]] of a process, by the minimizing the materials and energy required and [[waste]] produced, and is successfully applied in the production of [[Pharmaceutical drug|pharmaceuticals]] as well as [[Aroma compound|fragrances]], [[agrochemical]]s, [[pigment]]s, and [[food additive]]s.<ref name=":42">{{Cite web|last=Emily|first=Stoler|date=May 1, 2015|title=Non-covalent derivatives|url=https://repository.library.northeastern.edu/files/neu:rx915j570}}</ref> Warner holds patents based on NCD in many of these areas, most notably drugs to treat [[Nervous system disease|nervous system disorders]], additives to increase [[Recycling|recyclability]] of asphalt, and processes to reverse [[depigmentation]] in hair.<ref name=":72" />

NCD was also the impetus for a consequential meeting between Warner and the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)]], after the agency rejected a manufacturing model proposed by Polaroid based on the method.<ref name=":22" /> It was there that Warner was reunited with his long-time friend [[Paul Anastas]], and the two began to formulate the [[Green chemistry#Principles|Twelve Principles of Green Chemistry]].<ref name=":22" />

Warner became so infatuated with Non-Covalent Derivatization that his [[Massachusetts]] [[Vehicle registration plate|license plate]] bears the initials NCD.<ref name=":12" />

== Green Chemistry: Theory and Practice ==
The seminal work ''Green Chemistry: Theory and Practice'' was first conceived in a meeting at the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)]] about Non-Covalent [[Derivatization]] (NCD). When a new manufacturing model for [[Instant camera|instant photography]] based on NCD of [[hydroquinone]] was rejected by the EPA, [[Polaroid Corporation|Polaroid]] sent Warner to give a seminar on this new method.<ref name=":12" /> It was there that he met the branch chief at the Office of Pollution Prevention and Toxics, none other than his childhood and undergraduate friend [[Paul Anastas]].<ref name=":12" />

The introduction of the book highlights that many [[Ecological crisis|environmental crises]] in the twentieth century, from those depicted in [[Rachel Carson]]'s influential ''Silent Spring'' to the more recent events at [[Times Beach, Missouri|Times Beach]] and [[Love Canal]], stemmed from the poor practice of traditional industrial chemistry.<ref name=":62">{{Cite book|title=Green Chemistry: Theory and Practice|last1=Anastas|first1=Paul T.|last2=Warner|first2=John C.|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=1998}}</ref> As the [[environmental movement]] grew, the [[chemical industry]] was portrayed as the clear antagonist. Anastas and Warner argue that in the past, the role of the chemist in the [[Environmental impact assessment|environment]] was limited to site monitoring and remediation after an [[Chemical accident|accident]], but in a present where so many new chemicals are constantly introduced, it is now imperative that chemists assure that anything created is [[Toxicity|non-toxic]], before it is even synthesized.<ref name=":62" />

One of the most influential sections of the book outlines the [[Green chemistry#Principles|Twelve Principles of Green Chemistry]], which have served as the foundation for green chemistry curricula<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/greenchemistry/students-educators/academicprograms.html|title=Green Chemistry Academic Programs – American Chemical Society|website=American Chemical Society|language=en|access-date=December 10, 2017}}</ref> and the blueprint for chemical industry practice<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/greenchemistry/industry-business.html|title=Industry & Business – American Chemical Society|website=American Chemical Society|language=en|access-date=December 10, 2017}}</ref> throughout the world. The remainder of the book details how to design environmentally benign chemicals, from evaluating starting materials to examining concrete [[Toxicology|toxicological mechanisms]] and giving examples of green processes.<ref name=":62" />

''Green Chemistry: Theory and Practice'' did not invent the term green chemistry, which was coined in the early 1990s, but it was notable because it helped to define the motives and a common mission in the developing field.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal|last=Linthorst|first=J. A.|date=April 1, 2010|title=An overview: origins and development of green chemistry|journal=Foundations of Chemistry|language=en|volume=12|issue=1|pages=55–68|doi=10.1007/s10698-009-9079-4|issn=1386-4238|doi-access=free}}</ref> Within a few years after the book was released,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Linthorst |first=Johan Alfredo |url=https://eburon.nl/en/product/research-between-science-society-and-politics-ebook/ |title=Research between Science, Society and Politics: The History and Scientific Development of Green Chemistry |publisher=Eburon |year=2023 |isbn=9789463014342 |location=Utrecht |doi=10.26481/dis.20230209jl}}</ref> the number of [[Article (publishing)|papers]] and patents published that included the term green chemistry increased steadily.<ref name=":22" /> As of 2015, the book has been translated in fifteen different languages.<ref name=":22" />

== The Missing Elements ==
Warner has more recently presented a series of lectures at industrial and academic campuses throughout the country on the importance and legacy of green chemistry, titled ''The Missing Elements''.<ref name=":22" /> Warner will release a book based on these presentations in 2018, his first since the publication of ''Green Chemistry: Theory and Practice'' exactly twenty years prior.{{update inline|date=April 2019}}

==Personal life==
Warner has had at least one son, who died of liver failure due to [[biliary atresia]] at 2 years old. Warner cites the death of his son as a reason why he became more interested in studying green chemistry.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Warner |first=John |date=March 24, 2008 |title=Asking the Right Questions |url=https://www.npr.org/2008/03/24/88674284/asking-the-right-questions |access-date=2026-04-04 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref>

== Awards ==
Warner has been recognized for his pioneering work with several awards, including:
* 2002: "Distinguished Chemist of the Year Award" from the American Institute of Chemistry's Northeast Division<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.warnerbabcock.com/people/john-warner-ph-d/ | title=John Warner}}</ref>
* 2004: "Presidential Award for Excellence in Science, Mathematics and Engineering Mentorship" from the [[National Science Foundation]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=0429931|title=NSF Award Search: Award#0429931 – Individual Nomination for John C. Warner for Excellence in Science Mentoring|website=www.nsf.gov|access-date=February 28, 2017}}</ref>
* 2008: "Leadership in Science Award" (with Paul Anastas) from the Council of Scientific Society presidents<ref>{{cite web|url=http://thecssp.us/awards/leadership-citation | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141124220841/http://thecssp.us/awards/leadership-citation | archive-date=2014-11-24 | title=Leadership Citation}}</ref>
* 2011: "Environmental Merit Award" from the [[US EPA]]<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.epa.gov/aboutepa/epa-region-1-new-england | title=Environmental Merit Awards in New England| date=October 6, 2015}}</ref>
* 2011: "ACS Fellows Award" from the [[American Chemical Society|ACS]]<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/fellows/list-of-2011-acs-fellows.html | title=2011 ACS Fellows}}</ref>
* 2012: "Henry Maso Award" from the Society of Cosmetic Chemistry
* 2014: "Perkin Medal" from the [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]]<ref name="SCI Perkin Medal">{{cite web|title=SCI Perkin Medal|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/sci-perkin-medal|website=[[Science History Institute]]|access-date=March 24, 2018|date=May 31, 2016}}</ref>
* 2016: "AAAS-Lemelson Invention Ambassador" from the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] and [[Lemelson Foundation]]<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-and-lemelson-foundation-announce-2016-2017-class-invention-ambassadors|title=AAAS and The Lemelson Foundation announce the 2016–2017 Class of Invention Ambassadors|date=June 1, 2016|work=AAAS – The World's Largest General Scientific Society|access-date=February 28, 2017|language=en}}</ref>
* 2016: "Harry & Carol Mosher Award" from the ACS Santa Clara Valley Section<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/95/i7/Mosher-Award-goes-John-Warner.html?type=paidArticleContent|title=Mosher Award goes to John Warner {{!}} Chemical & Engineering News|last=Wang|first=Linda|website=cen.acs.org|access-date=February 28, 2017}}</ref>
